root_cause.text: In espintcp_sendmsg(), after calling espintcp_push_msgs() to flush a previous partial send, the code does not verify that the partial send has actually completed (i.e., emsg->len is zero), leading to reinitialization and reuse of ctx->partial while the old transfer still owns it, causing memory corruption and out-of-bounds read.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds a check `if (emsg->len) { err = -ENOBUFS; goto unlock; }` right after the call to espintcp_push_msgs() and before reinitializing the sk_msg, preventing reuse of an in-progress partial send. The commit description explicitly states that for blocking callers, espintcp_push_msgs() may return success even when the previous partial send is still pending, and then espintcp_sendmsg() would reinitialize and reuse ctx->partial while the old transfer still owns that state.

bic_trace_step.reason: In espintcp_sendmsg(), after calling espintcp_push_msgs(sk) to flush any previous partial send, the code does not verify that emsg->len is zero before reinitializing and reusing ctx->partial. Specifically, espintcp_push_msgs can return 0 (success) when it encounters EAGAIN without clearing emsg (see the branch `if (err == -EAGAIN) { ... return 0; }`). The subsequent `sk_msg_init(&emsg->skmsg)` then overwrites the partial state while the old transfer still owns the buffer, leading to memory corruption.
